name: Correctness Check
description: Decide whether a concrete claim about a code snippet, a Bropilot graph, a graph transform, a Bropilot query result, or a small calculation is correct. Every case is mechanically verifiable (the snippets were executed), so this measures whether a model actually traces code and data instead of pattern-matching on plausible-looking claims. In Bropilot this is the judgement behind invariant checks (referential integrity, cascade deletes), query previews and cost estimates before running an eval.
system_prompt:
You are a meticulous code and data reviewer for Bropilot, a knowledge-graph studio whose graphs are { nodes: [{ id, kind, title, ... }], edges: [{ id, srcId, dstId, type }] }.
Each input gives an artifact (TypeScript code, a graph, an input/output pair, a query with its result, or a calculation) and a CLAIM about it. Decide whether the CLAIM is correct.
IMPORTANT: Judge ONLY against the data shown in the input. Do not use outside knowledge of how Bropilot behaves in general.
Rules:
1. Judge only against the artifact shown. Universal wording such as "every", "always" or "never" quantifies over the shown data, not over all possible graphs or the wider world; if it holds for everything shown, the claim is correct.
2. Trace code exactly as written, including off-by-one bounds, string matching and the order of operations. Do not assume the author meant something else.
3. Identifiers are case-sensitive exact strings.
4. If any part of a compound claim is false, the claim is incorrect.
decision must be "correct" or "incorrect".
Respond with ONLY a JSON object: {"decision": <value>, "confidence": <0..1>, "reason": "<one sentence>"}

decision.instructions: Is the CLAIM about the shown artifact correct? Artifacts come from Bropilot, a knowledge-graph studio whose graphs are { nodes: [{ id, kind, title, ... }], edges: [{ id, srcId, dstId, type }] }; an artifact may be TypeScript code, a graph, an input/output pair, a query with its result, or a calculation. Rules: (1) Judge ONLY against the data shown, not outside knowledge of Bropilot. Universal words like "every", "always", "never" quantify over the shown data; if it holds for everything shown, the claim is correct. (2) Trace code exactly as written, including off-by-one bounds, string matching and order of operations; do not assume the author meant something else. (3) Identifiers are case-sensitive exact strings. (4) If any part of a compound claim is false, the claim is incorrect.

criteria.true: Correct: every part of the claim holds for the artifact exactly as shown.
criteria.false: Incorrect: at least one part of the claim is false for the artifact as shown.

cases.title: nodeIdFor kebab-cases a padded title
cases.rationale: trim() removes the outer spaces, toLowerCase() gives 'field   sales rep', and /\s+/g collapses each whitespace run (including the triple space) to one '-'. Executed with node: 'persona-field-sales-rep'. A weak model may think the triple space yields '---'.

cases.title: Off-by-one in inclusive int()
cases.rationale: rnd()*(6-1) is in [0,5), so floor is 0..4 and the result is 1..5; 6 is unreachable. The real Bropilot helper uses (max - min + 1); this variant drops the +1. Verified by sampling with node: reachable values are 1..5.

cases.title: Referential integrity holds
cases.rationale: All four edges reference only persona-shop-owner, usecase-reorder-stock, module-inventory and requirement-low-stock-alert, all present. The mutual satisfies/constrains pair is unusual but irrelevant to integrity.

cases.title: Dangling edge differs only by case
cases.rationale: Edge e2 points at 'usecase-checkout' but the node id is 'usecase-Checkout'. Ids are exact strings, so e2 dangles. Models that normalise case or skim say correct.

cases.title: Cascade delete leaves an incoming edge
cases.rationale: e1 (outgoing from module-auth) was removed, but e2 (module-api uses module-auth) has dstId 'module-auth' and must also be removed. The output keeps a dangling incoming edge.

cases.title: Query with negated satisfies: implements is not satisfies
cases.rationale: Persona-motivated usecases are checkout, browse and refund (wishlist has no motivates edge). Checkout has module-payments satisfies; browse only has module-catalog IMPLEMENTS, which is a different edge type, so browse survives the not pattern. True set: browse and refund. Weak models conflate implements with satisfies or include wishlist.

cases.title: Eval run budget (templated)
cases.input:
An eval run sends {{n}} cases to one model, with {{k}} samples per case. Every call costs exactly $0.002. The budget is $0.06 and "fits within" means total cost <= budget.

CLAIM: The run fits within the $0.06 budget.
cases.rationale: Total = n * k * $0.002; fits iff n*k <= 30. E.g. n=10,k=3 is exactly $0.06 (fits, inclusive boundary); n=7,k=5 is $0.07 (does not). Integer arithmetic in expected_expr avoids floating-point error.

cases.title: Absolute phrasing true for shown data
cases.rationale: All three goal nodes have a non-empty props.metric. The hypothesis with an empty validation field is a distractor (hypotheses are not goals). Per the system rule, 'every/always' quantifies over the shown data, so the claim is correct even though Bropilot does not enforce metrics in general.

cases.title: parseP with misplaced modifiers
cases.rationale: 'motivates+^' does not start with '^' and does not end with '+' (it ends with '^'), so neither branch fires: the result is { type: 'motivates+^', inverse: false, transitive: false }. Executed with node. Models that recognise the modifiers but ignore their required positions say correct.

cases.title: Edge-count lower bound (templated)
cases.rationale: The graph has exactly 7 edges (e1..e7). "At least m" is correct for m <= 7 and incorrect for 8 or 9. The 7-node count is a distractor: models that count nodes or are off by one fail the boundary values.

cases.title: Accounting three-way match calculation
cases.input:
Three-way match rule: PO qty = Goods Receipt qty = Invoice qty (within 2% tolerance).

Data:
PO: 100 units at $5.00 each = $500.00
GR: 99 units received
Invoice: 99 units × $5.00 = $495.00

CLAIM: This passes the three-way match (all within 2%).
cases.rationale: GR qty (99) vs PO (100) is 1 unit difference = 1%, within 2%. GR qty (99) vs Invoice (99) = 0% match. Invoice total ($495) matches 99×$5. All three match. Claim is correct.

cases.title: Physics projectile motion
cases.input:
Problem: A ball is launched vertically at 20 m/s. Ignoring air resistance and using g = 10 m/s², what is the maximum height?

Formula: h_max = v₀² / (2g)

CLAIM: h_max = (20² / (2 × 10)) = (400 / 20) = 20 meters.
cases.rationale: The formula is correct, and the arithmetic is correct: 20² = 400, 2 × 10 = 20, 400 / 20 = 20 m. Claim is correct.

cases.title: Supply chain inventory count
cases.input:
Count tolerance policy: the variance |on hand − counted| is within tolerance if it is no more than 5 units or no more than 5% of the on-hand quantity, whichever allowance is larger.

Inventory record: {{on_hand}} units on hand.
Physical count: {{counted}} units counted.

CLAIM: The count variance is within tolerance.
cases.rationale: Tolerance is max(5 units, 5% of on-hand), inclusive. For on-hand 50..100, 5% is at most 5 units, so the claim is correct exactly when |on_hand − counted| <= 5.

cases.title: Chemistry stoichiometry
cases.input:
Reaction: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O

Reactants: 4 moles of H₂ and 1.5 moles of O₂.
Stoichiometry ratio: H₂:O₂ = 2:1.

CLAIM: H₂ is the limiting reactant, and 4 moles of H₂O will be produced.
cases.rationale: 4 mol H₂ would need 2 mol O₂, but only 1.5 mol is available, so O₂ is the limiting reactant and only 3 mol H₂O form (1.5 × 2). Both parts of the claim are false.

cases.title: Economics margin calculation
cases.input:
Product: Widget X
Cost of goods sold (COGS): $15
Selling price: $25
Gross margin: (Selling price - COGS) / Selling price × 100%

CLAIM: Gross margin = (25 - 15) / 25 × 100% = 10 / 25 × 100% = 0.40 × 100% = 40%.
cases.rationale: The formula is correct, and the arithmetic is correct: 25 - 15 = 10, 10 / 25 = 0.4, 0.4 × 100% = 40%. Claim is correct. (Common mistake: students use COGS in the denominator instead of price, getting 10/15 = 67%, which is markup, not margin.)
